sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Sigyn** (*sigyn*) ​— Loyalty, ‌Wife of Loki ‌· Victorious ​girl-friend — is ​the wife ​of [[loki|Loki]] and ​the mother ​of his human ‌sons, the ​goddess who stands ​beneath the earth ‌holding a ​basin over her ‌bound husband's ​face, catching the ‌venom of ​the snake [[skadi|Skaði]] ​fastened above ​him — and ​the figure ​whose single act ‌of staying ​gave the medieval ‌North its ​explanation for earthquakes: ‌when she ​turns away to ‌empty the ​full basin, the ‌venom falls, ​Loki writhes, and ​the world ‌shakes.[^1]

Her attestation ‌is thin and ‌remarkably old. ​Snorri names her ​in his ‌catalogue of the ​Æsir with ​a wife's economy; ‌the skald ​Þjóðólfr of Hvinir, ​composing around ‌900, already used ​the kenning ‌'the burden of ​Sigyn's arms' ​for Loki, proving ​the marriage ​was proverbial a ‌century before ‌Iceland's conversion; and ​Völuspá, the ‌oldest poem of ​the Codex Regius, ​shows her ‌seated beside the ‌bound captive ‌'by no means ‌happy about ​her husband'.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores the ​name as **Sigyn** ​— identical ​to the ASCII ‌input, because ​normalized Old Norse ​writes no ​diacritic in this ‌name. The ​mechanical rule therefore ​places the ​name in Tier ‌2: nothing ​distinctive is lost ‌in transit, ​a statement about ‌orthography and never ​about the ‌goddess. The temple ‌is domain-less: ​the plain-ASCII sigyn.com ​is registered ​to a third ​party outside ‌the collection and ‌is watched ​for release.[^3]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 34 and 50, ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).

The Poetic Edda, trans. Carolyne Larrington, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014): Völuspá 35; Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál (Þjóðólfr of Hvinir, Haustlöng), trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Viking Society for Northern Research, 1998).
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Sigyn; PuniCodex lexicon record for sigyn (tier, domain status).

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Old Norse ‌as **Sigyn**, and ​it belongs ​to the goddess ​alone — ​the medieval record ​knows no human ‌bearer. Its ​etymology is probable ​rather than proven: ‌the standard ​analysis takes it ‌as a ​compound of *sigr*, ‌'victory', and *vina*, ​'girl-friend, female ​friend', yielding 'victorious ​girl-friend' — ​a name built ​on the same ‌friendly-woman element ​as the masculine ‌*vinr* compounds of ​the personal-name ‌stock.[^1] Cleasby–Vigfusson record ​the name ‌under Loki's wife; ​Simek and Orchard ‌give the ​same derivation with ​the usual ‌scholarly reserve, and ‌none of the ‌lexica proposes ​a serious rival.[^2]

​The ASCII form ‌is not ​a fallback here ​but the ‌form itself: normalized ​Old Norse writes ​five plain ‌Latin letters and ​a capital. ‌The Unicode restoration ​**Sigyn** therefore preserves ​nothing the ​ASCII alphabet loses, ​and the ‌mechanical rule classifies ‌the name Tier ​2 — ‌an orthographic fact, ​not a judgment ​on the ‌goddess. The y ‌marks a ‌rounded vowel in ‌sound, not a ​mark on ‌the page.

The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- **s** ​→ **S** — ‌Same, capitalized
​- **i** → ​**i** — Same
​- **g** ‌→ **g** — ​Same
- ​**y** → **y** ​— Same
- ‌**n** → ​**n** — Same

‌The project ​holds no domain ‌for this name. ​The plain-ASCII ‌**sigyn.com** is registered ‌to a third ​party outside ​the collection and ​is watched ​for release; this ‌temple claims nothing ‌it does ​not hold.[^3]

sources.citation: de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. Sigyn (sigr + *vina).

Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Sigyn; Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Sigyn; Orchard, Andy, Dictionary of Norse Myth and Legend (London: Cassell, 1997), s.v. Sigyn.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of the ‌name is **/ˈsiɣ.ʏn/** ‌— Old ​Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

- ​**Si-** — Voiceless ​alveolar sibilant [s] ​and short close ‌front unrounded ​[i], stressed on ​the first syllable ‌as in every ​Old Norse word; ‌the i is ​short, not ‌the long í
​- **-g-** — ​Intervocalic g is ​the voiced velar ​fricative [ɣ], a ​softened gh ‌as in Spanish ​lago, never a ‌hard stop between ​vowels
- **-yn** ‌— Short ​rounded front [ʏ], ‌the Old Norse ​y — round ‌the lips while ​saying i, as ​in German ‌hübsch — then ‌a clean voiced ‌alveolar nasal [n]

​For the modern ​speaker, the closest ‌approximation is: ​'SEE-ghyn' — two ​syllables with the ‌weight on the ​first, the g ​soft and gargled, ‌the y ​rounded and kept ‌short; never 'SIGH-in'.

​Kindred and historical ​forms of the ​name:

- **Old ​Norse** — ‌Sigyn, wife of ‌Loki; the name ​is attested only ‌for this goddess
​- **Younger Futhark** ​— ᛋᛁᚴᚢᚾ ‌(sikun), a normalized ‌phonetic reconstruction — ‌the short-twig row ‌distinguishes neither k ​from g nor ‌short from ​long vowels[^2]
- ​**Skaldic verse** — ​Sigyn in Þjóðólfr ‌of Hvinir's Haustlöng ​(c. 900): ​Loki is 'farmr ​Sigynjar arma', the ‌burden of Sigyn's ​arms[^3]
- **Modern ​Scandinavian** — Sigyn, ​a rare ‌but living given ​name in Sweden, ‌revived from the ​Edda

Sigyn is ‌Tier 2 because ​the restoration ‌preserves nothing the ‌ASCII form loses: ​no diacritic, no ​distinctive letter, no ​vowel length that ​spelling records. ‌English and Old ‌Norse write the ​name identically.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and grammar.
Zoëga, Geir T., A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1910), s.v. Sigyn.
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál (Þjóðólfr of Hvinir, Haustlöng), trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Viking Society for Northern Research, 1998).

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name ​is preserved ‌in medieval ‌Icelandic manuscripts in ​the Latin ​alphabet as ​**Sigyn** — Old ​Norse (North ​Germanic), attested 13th ‌c. CE ​in the ​Codex Regius and ‌related codices, ​recording material ‌centuries older.[^1] Before ​the Latin ‌bookhand, Old ​Norse names were ​carved in ​the Younger Futhark; ​no runic ​attestation of ‌this theonym survives, ​so the ‌manuscript form ​is the primary ‌witness. The ​runic rendering ‌is **ᛋᛁᚴᚢᚾ** (sikun).

​The scholarly ‌rendering proceeds step ​by step:

​- ᛋ ‌(sól) writes /s/.
‌- ᛁ ‌(ís) writes ​both /i/ and ​/e/ — ‌the short-twig ​row does not ​separate the ‌front vowels.
- ​ᚴ (kaun) ​writes both ‌/k/ and /g/ ​(and the ‌ng cluster) ​— the voiced ​stop of ​the manuscript ​form is invisible ‌to the ‌runes.
- The ​spelling sikun ‌is a ​normalized phonetic reconstruction: ​Younger Futhark ‌does not ‌distinguish voiced from ‌voiceless stops, ‌the rounded ​y from plain ‌u, or ​short from long ​vowels — ​the runic ‌form underspecifies exactly ​what the ​manuscript spelling ​records.[^2]
- The ‌name's etymology ​— *sigr* ​'victory' + *vina* ​'girl-friend', yielding ‌'victorious girl-friend' — ​is registered ‌in the ​lexica as probable, ‌not proven.[^3]

​The Unicode ‌restoration Sigyn is ‌therefore identical ​to the ​ASCII form — ​the restoration ​is a matter ‌of canonical ‌reference, not ​rescued orthography.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957).
Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957), runic appendix; Zoëga, Geir T., A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (Clarendon Press, 1910), s.v. Sigyn.
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. Sigyn; Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Sigyn.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Sigyn** is ​catalogued under Loyalty, ‌Wife of ‌Loki — and ​the pairing is ​exact: the sources ​give her no ​hall, no ​cult, no second ‌adventure; her whole ​divine identity is ​the marriage and ‌the vigil ​it becomes.[^1]

### ‌Loyalty

Hers is ​the corpus's purest ‌loyalty because ​it is loyalty ​without a cause ​the texts endorse: ​Loki's sentence is ​just, the ‌flyting's bill has ​come due, and ‌still she stands ​there. The ‌tradition never has ​her speak for ‌him; it has ​her stay by ‌him — ​a distinction the ​myth insists on.[^1]

‌### Wife of ‌Loki

Snorri introduces ‌her in ​three words — ​Loki's wife is ‌named Sigyn — ​and everything ​the tradition remembers ‌flows from the ​marriage: the human ​sons Nari and ‌Narfi, the ​kenning 'the burden ‌of Sigyn's arms', ​and the place ​beside him in ​the pit. ​Between [[angrboda|Angrboða]], the ‌giantess who bore ‌Loki the monsters, ​and Sigyn, ‌the wife within ​the walls, the ​tradition draws its ‌map of his ‌two households.[^1]

‌### The Basin

‌The venom basin ​is the only ‌office any source ​assigns her: ​holding it, filling ​it, emptying it. ‌An office measured ​in drops ​is still an ​office, and it ‌is the one ​mercy in the ​binding scene.[^1]

​### Earthquakes

When ‌the basin is ​full she must ‌turn away, ​and in that ‌gap the venom ​falls, Loki writhes ‌against the iron ‌bonds, and ​the earth shakes ​— 'those are ​now called earthquakes': ​her brief absence, ‌written into ‌the geology of ​the world.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 34 and 50, trans. Faulkes (1987).
The Poetic Edda, trans. Carolyne Larrington, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014): Lokasenna, prose epilogue.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
Sigyn's ​iconography ‌is the ‌sparsest ​in ​the ​Edda — ​one ​scene, ‌endlessly ​repeated, fixed ​around ‌a ​handful ‌of objects ​no ‌retelling ​can ​omit:[^1]

- ​**The ​venom ​basin** ‌— loyalty ​made ‌object: ​the ‌mercy she ​holds ‌over ​him, ‌measured drop ​by ​drop
‌- ‌**The venom-snake** ‌— ​Skaði's ​sentence, ‌fastened above ​Loki's ​face: ‌the ​fixed threat ​she ‌stands ​between
‌- **The ​iron ​bonds** ​— ​Nari's entrails ‌turned ‌to ​iron: ‌the binding ​her ​vigil ‌softens ‌but cannot ‌loose[^1]
‌- ​**The ‌three stones** ​— ​shoulders, ​loins, ‌and knees ​pinned ​in ​the ‌gorge: the ​fixed ​point ​of ‌her watch
​- ‌**The ​earthquake** ‌— the ​world ‌shaking ‌when ​the bowl ​is ​lifted: ​her ‌absence, counted ‌in ​tremors[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 50, trans. Faulkes (1987).
The Poetic Edda, trans. Carolyne Larrington, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014): Lokasenna, prose epilogue.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Sigyn's mythology is ​a naming, a kenning, a ‌stanza, and one great scene ‌— among the shortest dossiers ​in the corpus, and one ​of the oldest.

### The ​Wife of Loki (Gylfaginning 34)

​Snorri names her in the ​catalogue of the Æsir: [[loki|Loki]]'s ‌wife is named Sigyn, and ​their son is Nari or ​Narfi. No father, no hall, ‌no office — the wife ​exists to anchor Loki's human ‌family, set in the same ​chapter against the giantess [[angrboda|Angrboða]], ‌who bore him the wolf ​[[fenrir|Fenrir]], the World Serpent, and ​[[hel|Hel]]. That the marriage was ​already proverbial is proven by ​the skalds: Þjóðólfr of Hvinir's ​Haustlöng (c. 900) calls Loki ‌'farmr Sigynjar arma', the burden of ​Sigyn's arms — a kenning ‌that works only for an ​audience that already knows whose ‌wife she is.[^1]

### The ​Captive in the Grove of ‌Kettles (Völuspá 35)

The seeress ​of Völuspá, the oldest poem ‌of the Codex Regius, sees ​the punishment before it happens: ​a captive lying under the ‌grove of kettles, evil-minded, in ‌form like Loki — 'and ‌there sits Sigyn, by no ​means happy about her husband. ​Do you understand yet, or ‌what more?' Seated, sorrowing, and ​staying: the whole of her ​eddic portrait, complete in two ‌lines.[^2]

### The Flyting's Aftermath ​(Lokasenna, prose epilogue)

Lokasenna ends ​in a prose coda: Loki ‌is bound across three stones ​with the entrails of his ‌son Nari, while his son ​Narfi is turned into a ​wolf; [[skadi|Skaði]] fastens a venomous ​snake above his face. Sigyn ​sits there holding a basin ‌under the drip, and when ‌the basin is full she ​goes to pour it out ‌— but while she is ​gone the venom falls on ​Loki's face, and he writhes ‌so hard that the whole ‌earth shakes. Those, the text ‌says, are called earthquakes; there ‌he lies until Ragnarök.[^3]

### ​The Binding of Loki (Gylfaginning ‌50)

Snorri sets the same ​scene at the close of ​the Baldr cycle. After the ​death of [[baldr|Baldr]], the Æsir ‌hunt Loki to Franangr's falls, where ​he hides as a salmon ​and is caught in the ​net he himself invented. His ‌son Váli — not [[odinn|Óðinn]]'s ​son of the same name ​— is changed into a ​wolf and tears apart his ‌brother Nari; with Nari's entrails ​the gods bind Loki across ‌three stones, and the bonds ​turn to iron. Skaði fastens ‌the snake, and Sigyn, his ​wife, stands beside him holding ‌the basin — when she ‌turns away to empty it, ​the venom falls and the ​earth shakes. Snorri and the ​Lokasenna prose swap which son ​is gutted and which is ‌made a wolf; they do ‌not differ on the wife ​with the bowl.[^4]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 34, trans. Faulkes (1987); Skáldskaparmál (Haustlöng), trans. Faulkes (Viking Society, 1998).
Völuspá 35 (Poetic Edda), trans. Carolyne Larrington, The Poetic Edda, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014).
Lokasenna, prose epilogue (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 50, trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Sigyn's ​truest kin ‌are inside ‌the corpus ​itself. She ​is the ​mirror of ​[[nanna|Nanna]] — ​the two ‌wives of ​the Baldr ​catastrophe, one ‌following her ​dead husband ‌into the ​fire, the ‌other staying ​beside her ​living one ​in the ​pit: devotion ​answered by ‌death in ​the one, ‌by endurance ​without end ‌in the ​other. The ‌parallel is ​structural, ‌not borrowed ​— two ​tellings of ‌the northern ‌conviction that ‌the household ​pays what ​the battlefield ‌owes.[^1]

Cross-culturally, ​scholarship has ​been cool. ‌The bound-trickster ​scene has ​been set ‌beside Prometheus ​since the ‌nineteenth century, ​but no ​comparison touches ​the wife ​with the ‌bowl, and ‌the handbooks ​treat Sigyn ‌strictly within ​the Loki ​complex: her ‌attestation is ‌thin, her ‌etymology ‌only probable, ​and no ‌cult can ​be reconstructed ​from a ​basin held ‌over a ​bound god.[^2] ​What can ​be said ‌cleanly is ​that no ​other figure ​in the ‌Edda is ​defined so ‌entirely by ​a single ‌act of ​staying. Within ‌the corpus, ‌her related ​figures are ​the two ​households her ​story binds: ‌[[loki|Loki]], [[skadi|Skaði]], ‌[[angrboda|Angrboða]], and ​[[nanna|Nanna]].

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Sigyn, Loki.

Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Sigyn; Orchard, Andy, Dictionary of Norse Myth and Legend (London: Cassell, 1997), s.v. Sigyn.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
Sigyn's ​afterlife is ‌the afterlife ‌of one ​image. ​The medieval ​earthquake-theory — ​the ​earth shakes ‌when she ​lifts the ​bowl ‌— survived ​for centuries ‌as ​the North's ‌household explanation ​of tremors, ​and ​every retelling ​of Loki's ​punishment, ‌from the ​Kearys' Victorian ‌*Heroes of ​Asgard* ‌onward, keeps ​the wife ‌and ​the basin ‌at the ​centre of ​the ‌scene: it ‌is the ‌one ​moment of ​grace in ‌the flyting's ​long ​aftermath, and ‌illustrators have ​never ​been able ‌to leave ​it out.[^1]

‌Nineteenth-century ​romanticism made ​her the ​Edda's ​type of ‌wifely fidelity; ‌twentieth-century scholarship ​made ‌her the ​test case ​for ‌how much ‌a single ‌stanza and ‌a ​prose coda ‌can hold. ​The ​name itself ​went quietly ‌back into ​use ​— Sigyn ​is a ‌rare ​but living ​given name ​in Sweden ‌— ​and modern ‌Heathen and ​Ásatrú ‌communities honour ​her as ‌the goddess ‌of ​loyalty, fidelity, ​and endurance ​under ​an unjust ‌sentence: the ‌one who ​stays.[^2]

sources.citation: Keary, Annie, and Eliza Keary, The Heroes of Asgard: Tales from Scandinavian Mythology (London: Macmillan, 1857).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Sigyn.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
Sigyn ​has one ‌candidate image, ‌and it ​is famous. ​The Gosforth ​Cross in ​Cumbria, carved ​in the ‌first half ​of the ​tenth century, ‌carries a ​programme of ‌Ragnarök scenes ​that includes ‌a bound ​male figure ​with a ​smaller figure ​kneeling beside ​him holding ‌a bowl ​— standardly ‌interpreted as ​Loki bound ‌and Sigyn ​with the ‌basin, the ​one Viking-Age ‌monument that ​may show ​her at ‌her post.[^1] ‌The identification ‌is iconographic ​inference, not ​inscription: the ‌cross names ​nobody, and ​the reading ‌rests on ​the match ​with the ‌literary ​scene.

Otherwise ‌she is ​a wholly ​textual goddess: ​no runestone ​invokes her, ‌no votive ‌deposit names ​her, and ‌no other ​image can ​be securely ‌identified with ‌her. Her ‌attestation hangs ‌on the ​manuscript witnesses ‌of the ​Loki cycle ​— the ​Codex Regius ‌for Völuspá ​35 and ​the Lokasenna ​prose epilogue, ‌and the ​principal codices ​of Snorri's ​Edda for ‌Gylfaginning 34 ​and 50 ‌— with ​Þjóðólfr's Haustlöng ‌(c. 900), ​quoted in ‌Skáldskaparmál, proving ‌the kenning ​'the burden ​of Sigyn's ​arms' was ​already current ‌a century ‌before Iceland's ​conversion.[^2]

sources.citation: Bailey, Richard N., Viking Age Sculpture in Northern England (London: Collins, 1980), on the Gosforth Cross.
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Sigyn, Loki.

The account ​of Sigyn given in ‌this edition rests ‌on the witnesses and ​reference works listed ​below. Gylfaginning 34 and ​50 supply the ​narrative frame; Völuspá and ​the Lokasenna prose ‌the eddic attestation; Haustlöng ​the skaldic proof ​of the marriage's antiquity; ‌Cleasby–Vigfusson, Zoëga, and ​de Vries the name's ‌form and derivation, ​with Simek, Orchard, and ‌Lindow arbitrating attestation ​and motif, and Bailey ​the Gosforth iconography.

sections.label: Poetic Edda
sections.body:
The Poetic ​Edda gives ‌Sigyn exactly ‌two lines of ​verse and ​one prose ​coda — ​and both are ​load-bearing. In ‌Völuspá 35 ​the seeress, surveying ​the punishments ‌that precede ​Ragnarök, sees ‌a captive lying ​under the ‌grove of ​kettles, evil-minded, in ​form like ​[[loki|Loki]] — ​'and there sits ​Sigyn, by ‌no means ​happy about ‌her husband. Do ​you understand ‌yet, or ​what more?' It ‌is her ​only verse ‌appearance, and it ​is in ​the corpus's ‌oldest and ‌most authoritative poem: ‌seated, sorrowing, ​and staying ​was already her ‌whole character ​before Snorri ​was born.[^1]

‌The Lokasenna prose ​epilogue supplies ​the scene ‌the stanza implies. ​After the ‌flyting at ​Ægir's feast, Loki ​is caught ​and bound ​across three ‌stones with the ‌entrails of ​his son ‌Nari, while his ​son Narfi ​is turned ‌into a ‌wolf; [[skadi|Skaði]] fastens ‌the venomous ‌snake above ​his face, and ‌Sigyn sits ​holding the ​basin under the ​drip — ‌when she ​goes to ​empty it, the ​venom falls ‌and the ​earth shakes, 'and ​those are ​called earthquakes'.[^2] ‌Elsewhere the poems ​keep her ‌silence: Hyndluljóð's ​catalogue of ‌Loki's monstrous brood ​names [[angrboda|Angrboða]], ‌not Sigyn, ‌and no poem ​gives her ​a spoken ​word — ​her eddic voice ‌is the ‌fact of ​her presence.

sources.citation: Völuspá 35 (Poetic Edda), trans. Carolyne Larrington, The Poetic Edda, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014).
Lokasenna, prose epilogue (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014); Hyndluljóð (Loki's brood), trans. Larrington (2014).

sections.label: Prose Edda
sections.body:
The Prose ​Edda is ‌Sigyn's fullest ‌witness, and ​it frames ​her in three ​touches. Gylfaginning ​34 names ​her in ‌the catalogue ​of the Æsir ​— [[loki|Loki]]'s ‌wife, mother ​of Nari ‌or Narfi ​— in the ‌same breath ​that gives ​Loki his ​monstrous brood ​by [[angrboda|Angrboða]]: the ​two households ‌of the ​corpus's most ‌divided figure, the ​human family ‌within the ​walls and ‌the monsters ​without. Gylfaginning 50 ‌gives her ​the scene: ​after the ‌salmon-net at ‌Franangr and the ‌binding on ​the three ​stones, 'Sigyn, ‌Loki's wife, ​stands beside him ​and holds ‌a basin ​under the ​dripping venom', ‌and when she ​turns to ‌empty it, ​the venom ​falls, he ​writhes, and 'those ​are now ‌called earthquakes'.[^1]

‌Skáldskaparmál adds ​the two ‌archival facts. The ​ásynja þulur ​keep her ‌by name ‌in the ‌catalogue of the ‌goddesses — ​a deity ‌of one ​scene, filed ​with bureaucratic fidelity ​among the ‌ásynjur. And ​Þjóðólfr of ​Hvinir's Haustlöng, composed ​about 900 ‌and quoted ​for the ​Þjazi myth, ​calls Loki 'farmr ‌Sigynjar arma', ​the burden ‌of Sigyn's ​arms: a ‌kenning that presupposes ​the marriage ‌as common ‌knowledge three ​centuries before ​the Codex Regius ​was written ​— the ‌oldest datable ‌attestation of ​her name.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 34 and 50, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál (þulur; Þjóðólfr of Hvinir, Haustlöng), trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Viking Society for Northern Research, 1998).

sections.label: Runic Evidence
sections.body:
The ​runic corpus ‌contains ‌no ​invocation of ​the ​goddess Sigyn. ​No ​runestone asks ‌her ​favour, ​no amulet ‌bears ​her name, ‌and ​no inscription ‌yet ​found ​links a ​dedicant ​to her ​cult ‌— ​a silence ‌she ​shares with ‌most ​figures of ‌the ​Loki ‌cycle and ​one ​that marks ‌her ‌as a ‌literary-mythological ​figure ​rather than ‌an ​independently culted ​deity.[^1]

‌What ​can be ​said ‌runologically is ​the ‌rendering itself: ​in ​the ​Younger Futhark ​the ‌name would ‌have ​been ‌carved ᛋᛁᚴᚢᚾ ​(sikun) ​— a ‌normalized ‌phonetic reconstruction, ‌since ‌the ​sixteen-rune row ‌distinguishes ​neither k ​from ​g nor ‌short ​from ​long vowels, ​and ‌thus underspecifies ​exactly ​the ​features the ‌manuscript ​spelling preserves. ‌No ​Viking-Age carving ‌of ​the ‌theonym is ‌known; ​the manuscript ​spelling ​of the ​Eddas ‌remains ‌the primary ​witness.[^2]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Sigyn, Loki.
Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957), runic appendix.

sections.label: Sagas & Medieval Sources
sections.body:
Beyond ​the Eddas, ‌Sigyn's medieval ‌afterlife ​is a ​study ​in near-absence ​— and ​in ‌what survives ​anyway. ​Saxo Grammaticus, ‌who gives ​[[nanna|Nanna]] ‌a whole ​second life ‌in ​Denmark, never ​mentions ​her: the ​Gesta Danorum's ​Loki-figure ‌(the bound ​Utgartha-Locus) ‌carries no ​wife with ‌a ​bowl, and ‌the ​Danish tradition ‌preserves no ​counter-version ​of her ‌vigil.[^1]

What ‌the ‌skaldic record ​preserves ​instead is ‌the proof ​of ​her antiquity. ‌Þjóðólfr ​of Hvinir's ​Haustlöng, composed ‌about ​900, already ‌calls [[loki|Loki]] ​'farmr ​Sigynjar arma' ​— ​the burden ‌of Sigyn's ‌arms ​— in ‌the ​midst of ​the Þjazi ‌episode: ‌a kenning ‌that only ‌works ​for an ‌audience ​to whom ​'Sigyn's husband' ​needs ‌no explanation. ​Between ​the seeress's ​two lines ‌in ​Völuspá and ​the ​skald's kenning, ‌the wife ​with ‌the bowl ​is attested ‌in ​the two ‌oldest ‌strata of ​the whole ​corpus, ​and everywhere ​after ‌only by ‌the scene ​itself.[^2]

sources.citation: Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum, trans. Peter Fisher, ed. Hilda Ellis Davidson (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1979); Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide (Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Sigyn.
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál (Þjóðólfr of Hvinir, Haustlöng), trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Viking Society for Northern Research, 1998).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Sigyn ​is the ‌Edda's one ‌study of ​fidelity without ​hope. Every ​other loyalty ​in the ​corpus has ‌a horizon: ​vengeance will ​come, the ‌ransom may ​succeed, Ragnarök ‌will end ​it. ‌Hers has ​none — ​the binding ​is until ​the world's ​end, the ‌snake does ​not sleep, ‌the basin ​fills at ‌the same ​rate forever. ‌And the ​tradition ‌is pitilessly ​exact about ​the terms ‌of her ‌mercy: it ‌is not ​that she ​fails. It ‌is that ​she must ​sometimes put ‌the bowl ​down.[^1]

In ​that gap ‌the ​whole myth ‌lives. The ​Norse imagination ​looked at ​the shaking ​earth and ‌did not ‌see a ​god's rage ‌or a ​giant's hammer ​— it ‌saw the ‌moments when ‌a ‌devoted woman ​turns away ‌to empty ​a basin. ​Loki deserves ​his sentence; ‌the texts ​never pretend ​otherwise. Sigyn ​is not ‌there to ​acquit him. ​She is ​there ‌because love ​does not ‌consult the ​verdict, and ‌the oldest ​poem in ‌the collection ‌already knew ​it: there ​sits Sigyn, ​by no ​means happy ‌— and ‌there she ​sits.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 50, trans. Faulkes (1987); Völuspá 35, trans. Larrington (2014).
